Equal Angles In Two Circles

GeometryCircles
Game: Two circles overlap and a straight line touches one at P and crosses the other at A and B; watch two corner angles that stay the same.
How to play: Drag the dots S, T, RB and RS with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Press Names, Statement, Hint or Extra to show the labels and the marked angles.
Look for the math

Two circles cross at S and T. One circle has a point P on it that lies inside the other circle. A straight chord AB of the outer circle just touches the inner circle at P. The page claims ∠ASP = ∠BTP and ∠ATP = ∠BSP. Drag the four points and see for yourself: it is a picture to explore, not a game to win. The live cut-the-knot page still embeds Bogomolny's Java applet; this page draws the same construction with draggable points.

One angle, two names

A tangent to the inner circle at P and the chord PT make the same angle as the one PT makes on the opposite arc: ∠PST = ∠BPT (the page calls this angle u when Hint is on). The angle sum in triangle BPT is then

∠PBT + ∠BPT + ∠BTP = 180°.

S and T lie on the outer circle with A and B, so ABTS is a cyclic quadrilateral: ∠AST + ∠ABT = 180°. Split the first angle at P and use ∠PST = ∠BPT:

∠ASP + ∠PST + ∠ABT = 180°
∠PBT + ∠BPT + ∠BTP = 180°
⇒ ∠ASP = ∠BTP.

The second pair

Angles standing on the same arc give ∠ASB = ∠ATB in the outer circle. Split them at P: ∠ASB = ∠ASP + ∠BSP and ∠ATB = ∠ATP + ∠BTP. The equal sums and the first pair ∠ASP = ∠BTP leave ∠ATP = ∠BSP. Press Extra to see the dashed lines SB and TA that frame this second pair.

How this differs from its siblings

Here the chord AB touches the inner circle at just one point P; there is no second crossing Q. The applet Equal Angles In Crossed Circles II replaces that tangency by a chord cutting the other circle at P and Q, and claims ∠ASP = ∠BTQ and ∠ATP = ∠BSQ. Equal Chords in Crossing Circles is different again: two lines through a crossing point, a claim about equal chord lengths, and switches for adjusting circles or chords. This applet keeps its own four checkboxes — names, statement, hint and extra — and its larger-radius circle is always called the outer one.

What the checks found

The logic test compares every field with a second transcription of the applet's own bytecode on the opening picture, 360 sweeps of the handles, and over 4,000 random and near-opening drawings. On every drawing that matches the page's description — P on the inner circle and inside the outer one — both angle pairs agree to better than a billionth of a radian, as do the tangent–chord step and the two 180° angle sums. The claim is not unconditional: pull P outside the outer circle and the two marked angles can become supplementary instead of equal (they add to 180°); the test pins down such a case. Two faithful quirks stay: when S and T come within one unit the applet draws ST as the tangent at T instead of stopping, and when the three points defining a circle are collinear there is no picture and the previous drawing is kept.

Turn on Statement and Hint, then drag RS a little: the two angles marked x stay the same while the proof letters u, v, y and z move. Now pull P outside the other circle and watch the x angles part company.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
